title: Product quantization (PQ)
summary: How PQ compresses vectors into a few bytes by k-means per sub-vector, scores codes with per-query lookup tables (ADC vs SDC), scales with IVF residuals, and is refined by OPQ, fast scan and ScaNN.
outcomes: Explain why one huge k-means codebook is infeasible and how a product of m small codebooks gives (k*)^m centroids
Encode a vector with PQ and compute its code size in bits and bytes
Build an ADC lookup table for a query and score codes by summing m lookups
Explain why ADC beats SDC and why IVFADC encodes residuals and probes w lists
Choose code size, nprobe, OPQ, 4-bit fast scan and re-ranking for a memory budget

lessons.title: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes

blocks.md:
Recall from the previous course: an ANN index such as HNSW finds near neighbors without scanning everything, but it still keeps every full vector in RAM to compute distances. That is where memory goes. One billion 768-dimensional embeddings stored as float32 take 768 x 4 = 3,072 bytes each, about 3.07 TB in total, before any graph links.

This course is about **product quantization (PQ)**, introduced by Jegou, Douze and Schmid (TPAMI 2011). PQ replaces each vector with a short **code** of a few bytes and still estimates distances to a query, directly from the codes.

A **quantizer** maps a vector to the nearest of $k$ representative vectors, called **centroids**; the list of centroids is the **codebook**. Store the centroid index instead of the vector and you need only $\log_2 k$ bits. k-means (Lloyd's algorithm) learns a good codebook.

The catch is scale. For a 64-bit code you need $k = 2^{64}$ centroids. The paper points out that you cannot train that: k-means needs several times $k$ training samples, the cost is prohibitive, and there is not enough memory on Earth to store $2^{64}$ centroids.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you split a 128-dimensional vector into 8 chunks of 16 dimensions and give each chunk its own codebook of 256 centroids. How many distinct reconstructed vectors can the 8 codes describe, and how many centroids do you actually store?
blocks.reveal: The code picks one centroid per chunk independently, so it can describe $256^8 = 2^{64}$ distinct vectors. You only store $8 \times 256 = 2{,}048$ small centroids of 16 dimensions each. That gap, a huge implicit codebook built from a few small explicit ones, is the whole trick of product quantization.

blocks.md:
**Product quantization** splits a $D$-dimensional vector into $m$ **sub-vectors** of $D^* = D/m$ dimensions each (so $D$ must be a multiple of $m$). Each sub-vector position $j$ gets its own small k-means codebook $C_j$ with $k^*$ centroids, called a **sub-quantizer**. A vector is stored as the $m$ indices of its nearest sub-centroids.

The full codebook is the Cartesian product $C = C_1 \times \dots \times C_m$, which is where the name comes from. A reconstructed vector is the concatenation of the chosen sub-centroids.

blocks.caption: Equation 8 of the PQ paper: each sub-vector u_j is quantized by its own sub-quantizer q_j.

blocks.title: Splitting an 8-dim vector into 4 sub-vectors and a 1-byte code

scenes.caption: A toy database vector y2 with D = 8 float32 values: 32 bytes. We will use m = 4 sub-vectors of D* = 2 dimensions and k* = 4 centroids per sub-quantizer.
Consecutive dimensions are grouped: dims 1-2 form u1, dims 3-4 form u2, and so on. Each group has its own codebook trained only on that slice of the data.
Each sub-vector is replaced by the index of its nearest centroid in its own codebook (next lesson computes these). y2 gets the code (2, 3, 2, 2).
With k* = 4, each index needs log2(4) = 2 bits, so the code is 4 x 2 = 8 bits = 1 byte, a 32x reduction. The 4 codebooks can jointly describe 4^4 = 256 different reconstructions.

blocks.tex: \text{code length} = m \log_2 k^* \text{ bits}, \qquad |C| = (k^*)^m, \qquad \text{codebook storage} = m\,k^*\,D^* = k^* D \text{ floats}
blocks.caption: The paper's resource counts. Codebook storage grows with k* but not with the number of database vectors.

blocks.md:
The paper's usual setting is $k^* = 256$ (one byte per sub-vector) and $m = 8$, a 64-bit code. For a 128-dim SIFT descriptor (512 bytes as float32) that is 8 bytes, a 64x reduction. In Faiss the same thing is written `PQ8` (8 sub-quantizers, 8 bits each by default).

The plot below shows what this means at scale. Faiss's IVF variant (lesson 4) also stores an 8-byte id per vector, so we draw that too.

blocks.title: Index memory vs number of vectors

scenes.caption: At 1 billion vectors of 768 dims, raw float32 needs 3,072 GB; 64-byte PQ codes need 64 GB, or 72 GB with 8-byte ids. That is the difference between a cluster and one large server.
Shrinking codes to 16 bytes cuts memory 4x again (16 GB per billion codes), but as later lessons show, recall drops as codes get shorter.
Simplified model: it counts only vectors or codes. Real indexes add codebooks, coarse centroids and list overhead, which are small next to the codes at this scale.

blocks.md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

blocks.question: You use m = 16 sub-quantizers with k* = 256 on 512-dim float32 vectors. How many bytes does each PQ code take, and what is the compression ratio?
options: 16 bytes, 128x smaller than 2,048 bytes
256 bytes, 8x smaller
64 bytes, because each sub-vector stores 32 dims
2 bytes, because 16 codes x 1 bit
blocks.explain: Each of the 16 indices takes log2(256) = 8 bits = 1 byte, so 16 bytes. The raw vector is 512 x 4 = 2,048 bytes, so the ratio is 128x. The sub-vector width (32 dims) changes the codebook size, not the code size.

blocks.question: Why can't we just run k-means with 2^64 centroids to get 64-bit codes directly?
options: k-means only works in two dimensions
64-bit integers overflow on most CPUs
Training needs several times 2^64 samples and the centroids alone could not be stored
The resulting codes would be longer than 64 bits
blocks.explain: The PQ paper's argument: learning needs many more samples than centroids, the assignment cost scales with k, and storing D x 2^64 floats is impossible. Product quantization gets the same number of reproduction values from m small codebooks.

lessons.title: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector

blocks.md:
Training a product quantizer is just **m independent k-means runs**. Take a training set, slice out sub-vector $j$ from every training vector, and run k-means with $k^*$ centroids on those slices. Repeat for each $j$. The cost is $m$ times one small k-means of $k^*$ centroids in $D^*$ dimensions.

k-means alternates two steps until it settles: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. These are the two Lloyd optimality conditions the paper relies on. k-means only finds a local optimum, so results depend on the starting centroids.

Our toy: 40 training vectors of 8 dimensions, values rounded to one decimal, generated with a fixed random seed from a few clusters per 2-dim slice. We ran k-means with $k^* = 4$ on each of the 4 slices (numpy, fixed seed) and rounded the centroids to one decimal. Every number below is computed from those rounded values. For simplicity the toy database is the training set; real systems train on a separate sample.

blocks.title: The four learned codebooks (4 centroids of 2 dims each)

scenes.caption: Each row is one sub-quantizer: 4 centroids, each a 2-dim point (columns a and b). That is all the model we store: 4 x 4 x 2 = 32 floats, shared by every database vector.
Codebook u2 is crowded: its centroids lie within about 2.2 units of each other, while u3 spans more than 4 units. k-means adapts each codebook to the spread of its own slice.
Encoding y2 picks c2 in u1, c3 in u2, c2 in u3 and c2 in u4. Concatenating those cells gives the reconstruction q(y2).

blocks.md: **Encoding** a vector applies the first Lloyd condition per slice: for each $j$, compute the squared distance from $u_j(y)$ to each of the $k^*$ centroids of $C_j$ and keep the index of the smallest. The cost is $k^* D$ multiply-adds per vector, independent of the database size.

blocks.title: Encoding y2: squared distance to each centroid, per sub-vector

scenes.caption: u1(y2) = (0.5, 1.8). Distances to the u1 centroids: 7.25, 2.26, 0.05, 9.25. The nearest is c2 = (0.6, 1.6), so the first index is 2.
u2(y2) = (1.1, 0.1). Nearest is c3 = (1.3, -0.1) at 0.08, with c2 at 0.26 close behind. Index 3.
u3(y2) = (0.7, 2.5). c2 = (0.7, 2.0) wins at 0.25; c0 and c1 are far away. Index 2.
u4(y2) = (-0.3, 1.8). A close call: c2 at 0.13 beats c1 at 0.18. Index 2. The code for y2 is (2, 3, 2, 2).

blocks.title: Reconstruction and quantization error of y2

scenes.caption: The original vector. The index stores only the code (2, 3, 2, 2), so at search time the best we can know about y2 is its reconstruction.
q(y2) concatenates u1:c2, u2:c3, u3:c2, u4:c2. Close, but not equal.
Per-dimension squared error. The total is 0.51, about 3.5% of the squared norm of y2 (14.78). Over all 40 toy vectors the mean squared error is 1.03, versus a mean squared norm of 12.1.

blocks.md:
Because the sub-spaces are orthogonal, the total squared error is simply the sum of the per-slice errors: $\text{MSE}(q) = \sum_j \text{MSE}(q_j)$. This is why each codebook can be trained alone: minimizing each slice's k-means error minimizes the whole.

It also explains a weakness. A fixed $k^*$ per slice works best when every slice carries comparable energy (variance). If one slice holds most of the variance, its codebook is overloaded while others waste bits. The paper notes that consecutive components are often correlated and are better quantized together, so it keeps the natural order rather than shuffling dimensions; lesson 5 returns to this.

Common misconception: a PQ code is a lossless compression of the vector. It is not. Two different vectors with the same code are indistinguishable to the index, and every distance computed from codes inherits the quantization error.

blocks.question: A colleague trains one PQ codebook per sub-vector but forgets to use the same dimension split at encoding time (they split the database vectors in a different order). What happens?
options: Nothing, because k-means is permutation invariant
Codes are still valid but 2x larger
Every sub-vector is matched against a codebook learned on different dimensions, so reconstructions and distances are garbage
Only the first sub-vector is affected
blocks.explain: Codebook C_j only knows the distribution of slice j. Feeding it a different slice produces arbitrary nearest-centroid choices. The split (and any rotation applied before it) is part of the model and must be identical for training, encoding and querying.

blocks.question: For the same 64-bit budget on 128-dim SIFT, which setting did the PQ paper find gives lower quantization error?
options: m = 64 sub-quantizers with 2 centroids each
Both give exactly the same error because the bits are equal
m = 128 scalar quantizers with 1 bit each
m = 8 sub-quantizers with 256 centroids each
blocks.explain: Figure 1 of the paper: for a fixed number of bits, fewer sub-quantizers with more centroids each give lower distortion, because each codebook captures more of the joint structure within its slice. The cost is that k* = 256 makes codebook training and table building more expensive than k* = 4.

lessons.title: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC

blocks.md:
Now the payoff: estimating distances without decompressing. The paper gives two estimators for the distance between a query $x$ and a database vector $y$.

- **Symmetric distance computation (SDC)**: quantize both, and use $d(q(x), q(y))$. Per sub-vector the squared distance between two centroids is read from a precomputed $k^* \times k^*$ table.
- **Asymmetric distance computation (ADC)**: quantize only the database vector, and use $d(x, q(y))$. The query stays exact.

blocks.caption: ADC (Equation 13). The m x k* squared distances from each query sub-vector to each sub-centroid are computed once per query, before the scan.

blocks.md:
For ADC, the query preparation builds a **lookup table** (LUT) $T[j][i] = \|u_j(x) - c_{j,i}\|^2$: $m$ rows, $k^*$ columns, costing $k^* D$ operations once per query. Scoring a database code is then $m$ table reads and $m - 1$ additions. No vector arithmetic happens per database item, and square roots are skipped because they do not change the ranking.

Our toy query is $x = (0.2, 1.8, 0.8, -0.4, 0.5, 1.9, -1.1, 1.8)$.

blocks.title: ADC lookup table for query x (squared distances)

scenes.caption: Row j holds the squared distance from query slice u_j(x) to each centroid of codebook j. Example: u1(x) = (0.2, 1.8) vs c2 = (0.6, 1.6) gives 0.16 + 0.04 = 0.20. 16 numbers, computed once.
Score y2 with code (2, 3, 2, 2): read T[1][2] + T[2][3] + T[3][2] + T[4][2] = 0.20 + 0.34 + 0.05 + 1.25 = 1.84. The exact squared distance is 1.47.
Score y0 with code (0, 3, 2, 0): 5.78 + 0.34 + 0.05 + 4.05 = 10.22 (exact: 11.16). Same cost, 4 lookups, regardless of D.
Score y1 with code (2, 0, 3, 3): 0.20 + 2.89 + 2.61 + 7.25 = 12.95 (exact: 12.14). The ranking y2, y0, y1 matches the exact ranking.

blocks.title: The ADC scan loop

scenes.caption: The table is built once per query. The database is just small integer codes.
y0: four lookups summed. Its estimate 10.22 becomes the best so far.
y1 scores 12.95, which is worse, so the best is unchanged.
y2 scores 1.84 and wins. Real systems keep a max-heap of the K best instead of one best.

blocks.prompt: Now quantize the query too (SDC). x encodes to (2, 2, 2, 1). Using centroid-to-centroid tables, will the ranking of y0 (exact 11.16) and y1 (exact 12.14) stay correct?
blocks.reveal: No. SDC gives y0 = 7.54 + 0.50 + 0 + 4.21 = **12.25** and y1 = 0 + 2.41 + 2.18 + 4.81 = **9.40**, so y1 now looks closer than y0, which is wrong. Quantizing the query adds a second source of error. ADC kept the order (10.22 vs 12.95). Across all 40 toy vectors, SDC also swaps the 3rd and 4th true neighbors, while ADC's top 4 match the exact top 4.

blocks.title: Exact vs ADC vs SDC squared distances for 6 toy vectors

scenes.caption: Exact squared distances from x. True order: y2, y5, y0, y1, y3, y4.
ADC estimates: 10.22, 12.95, 1.84, 23.61, 31.00, 6.95. Off by up to 4 units, yet the order is preserved.
SDC estimates: 12.25, 9.40, 0.87, 25.20, 27.65, 4.96. y0 and y1 are now swapped: query quantization error broke the ranking.

blocks.md:
The paper bounds the error. By the triangle inequality, ADC's mean squared distance error is at most the quantizer's MSE; for SDC the bound is $2 \times$ MSE. Both estimators are also **biased low** on average; the paper derives a correction term (the expected cell distortion) but finds it raises variance and gives worse search results, so it recommends the uncorrected estimator for ranking.

Empirically, on SIFT with $m = 8$, ADC with $k^* = 64$ matched SDC with $k^* = 256$, at the same speed. The only advantage of SDC is that the query is a code too, which rarely matters.
ADC = exact query, quantized database. Per query you build an $m \times k^*$ table once, then each database vector costs $m$ lookups and adds. This is why PQ scans are fast and why everyone uses ADC.

blocks.question: With m = 8 and k* = 256, how many table entries does the ADC lookup table hold per query, and how many lookups score one database vector?
options: 2,048 entries, 8 lookups
256 entries, 256 lookups
65,536 entries, 8 lookups
8 entries, 256 lookups
blocks.explain: The table has m x k* = 8 x 256 = 2,048 entries (one per sub-quantizer and centroid). Each database code has 8 indices, so scoring it reads 8 entries. The 256 x 256 = 65,536 figure is the size of one SDC centroid-to-centroid table.

blocks.question: Your ADC distances are consistently smaller than the true distances. Is that a bug?
options: Yes: ADC should be unbiased because the query is exact
Yes: you forgot the square roots
No: the paper shows the estimator underestimates on average, and ranking does not need the bias removed
No: but you must add the correction term or recall collapses
blocks.explain: Jegou et al. show d(x, q(y)) underestimates on average. Adding the expected distortion removes the bias but increases variance, and in their experiments the corrected version gave inferior search results. Correct it only if you need the distance values themselves, for example for a radius threshold.

lessons.title: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes

blocks.md:
ADC still touches every code. At a billion vectors and 8 lookups each, that is 8 billion lookups per query. The paper's fix is **IVFADC**: an inverted file with asymmetric distance computation.

A **coarse quantizer** $q_c$ is an ordinary k-means with $k'$ centroids (the paper uses $k'$ from 1,000 to 1,000,000 for SIFT). It partitions the database into $k'$ **inverted lists**. A query scans only the lists of its $w$ nearest coarse centroids, about $n \times w / k'$ entries when lists are balanced. Faiss calls $k'$ `nlist` and $w$ `nprobe`.

The second idea is to encode the **residual** instead of the vector:

$r(y) = y - q_c(y)$

The residual has much less energy than the vector itself, so the same PQ budget describes it more precisely. The paper's analogy: the coarse centroid supplies the most significant bits, the PQ code the least significant ones. One product quantizer is trained on residuals pooled from all cells, rather than one per cell, which would cost $k' \times D \times k^*$ floats.

nodes.label:
LUT for
x - qc per list

scenes.caption: Indexing: y is assigned to its nearest coarse centroid, the residual is PQ-encoded, and (id, code) is appended to that centroid's list. The query path is hidden for now.
Why residuals: y minus its coarse centroid is small, so the PQ codebooks (trained on residuals from all cells) spend their bits on fine detail instead of on which region y lives in.
Search: the query finds its w nearest coarse centroids (multiple assignment). The database is not multiply assigned, which would multiply memory.
For each probed list, the query residual x - qc changes, so a fresh m x k* table is built per list. Then only that list's codes are scanned.
Each estimated distance enters a fixed-size max-heap only if it beats the current K-th best. Only the scan step grows with the database.

blocks.caption: Equation 31: ADC applied to the query residual against the stored residual code.

blocks.md: The paper's GIST experiment (1M vectors, 960 dims, 64-bit codes, 500 queries) shows the effect. Exhaustive ADC compared 1,000,991 codes in 17.2 ms per query with recall@100 of 0.652. IVFADC with $k' = 1024, w = 8$ compared only 27,818 codes in 8.8 ms and reached 0.682, because residual codes are more accurate. With $w = 1$ it took 1.5 ms but recall fell to 0.308: the true neighbor often sits in a nearby cell, and a neighbor in an unvisited list is lost for good.

blocks.title: Our synthetic test: residual vs raw codes (IVF with 64 lists)

scenes.caption: 1-recall@10 (true nearest neighbor in the top 10) with nprobe = 1, scanning 2.1% of the database. Residual encoding lifts 8-byte codes from 0.41 to 0.70.

nprobe = 4 (9.9% scanned): 0.42, 0.71, 0.88, 0.96. Simplified: synthetic 64-dim data with well-separated clusters (20,000 vectors, 500 queries), so one list already holds most true neighbors; real data needs larger nprobe.

blocks.md: In Faiss this is `IndexIVFPQ(quantizer, d, nlist, M, nbits)`, or the factory string `IVF4096,PQ16`. Encoding by residual is the default (`by_residual = true`). Each stored entry costs the code, ceil(M x nbits / 8) bytes, plus an 8-byte id. With L2 distance an optional precomputed table (`use_precomputed_table`, size nlist x M x ksub) speeds up building the per-list tables at some memory cost.

blocks.code:
import faiss, numpy as np

d, nlist, M, nbits = 768, 4096, 64, 8
xt = np.random.rand(200_000, d).astype('float32')  # training sample
xb = np.random.rand(1_000_000, d).astype('float32')

quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)            # coarse quantizer
index = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(quantizer, d, nlist, M, nbits)
index.train(xt)       # k-means for coarse centroids, then PQ on residuals
index.add(xb)         # 64-byte code + 8-byte id per vector

index.nprobe = 16     # w: lists scanned per query
D, I = index.search(xb[:5], 10)
blocks.caption: IVFADC in Faiss. Equivalent factory: faiss.index_factory(768, "IVF4096,PQ64"). Random data is only a placeholder.

blocks.md: Raising code size cannot fix a too-small nprobe. The paper notes that increasing the code length is useless if w is not big enough, because neighbors outside the probed lists are never scored. Tune nprobe first, then code size.

blocks.question: An IVFPQ index with nlist = 1024 and PQ64 has poor recall. Profiling shows the true nearest neighbor is usually in the 3rd or 4th nearest list. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to PQ128 codes
Reduce nlist to 64 so lists are bigger
Turn off residual encoding
Increase nprobe from 1 to 8
blocks.explain: Neighbors in unprobed lists are never scored, so better codes cannot find them. Raising nprobe scans those lists. Shrinking nlist also captures them but scans a much larger fraction per probe; the paper finds that for a fixed fraction visited, more lists with more probes is more accurate.

blocks.question: Why does IVFADC build a new lookup table for each probed list instead of one table per query?
options: Each list has its own PQ codebook
The codes are encoded relative to that list's coarse centroid, so the query residual x - qc changes per list
Faiss recomputes tables to avoid cache misses
The table depends on the database vector id
blocks.explain: The stored codes describe y - qc(y). To compare, the query must be expressed relative to the same centroid, x - qc. The codebook is shared across lists, but the query sub-vectors differ, so the m x k* distances differ.

lessons.title: Code size vs recall, and refinements: OPQ, fast scan, ScaNN

blocks.md: How much recall does a given code size buy? We ran PQ ourselves on synthetic data: 64-dim vectors from 100 Gaussian clusters with a decaying variance spectrum, 10,000 training vectors, 20,000 database vectors and 500 queries, exhaustive search, k-means with 20 iterations (numpy, fixed seed). The metric is **1-recall@10**: the fraction of queries whose true nearest neighbor appears in the top 10, the paper's recall@R with R = 10.

scenes.caption: ADC with 8-bit sub-quantizers (M = 4, 8, 16, 32). Recall climbs steeply with code size: 0.24, 0.42, 0.88, 1.00.
SDC on the same codes: 0.21, 0.33, 0.78, 1.00. Quantizing the query costs recall at every size, most at mid sizes.

ADC with 4-bit sub-quantizers at the same byte budget (M = 8 to 64): 0.24, 0.51, 0.87, 1.00. Similar or better recall here, but on real data Faiss reports PQ32x4 is much less accurate than PQ16x8 at the same memory; 4-bit wins on speed via SIMD tables.

blocks.md: On real SIFT data the paper found that for a fixed number of bits, fewer sub-quantizers with more centroids generally win, although MSE understates how well many small sub-quantizers do on search. In practice, recall is tuned with code size, nprobe and a **re-ranking** step: fetch more candidates than needed (say 100) using codes, then recompute exact distances for those few from full vectors kept on disk or in a smaller precise code. Faiss exposes this as `IndexRefine` or the `Refine(...)` and `RFlat` factory suffixes.

**OPQ (Optimized Product Quantization)**, Ge, He, Ke and Sun (CVPR 2013), attacks the dimension-split problem from lesson 2. It learns an orthogonal rotation $R$ applied before PQ, jointly with the codebooks, to minimize quantization distortion. The non-parametric method alternates: fix $R$ and run PQ k-means; fix the codebooks and solve for $R$ in closed form with an SVD (an orthogonal Procrustes problem). The parametric method assumes Gaussian data: align by PCA, then greedily assign eigenvalues to $m$ buckets so the product of eigenvalues per sub-space is balanced (**Eigenvalue Allocation**).

Why it matters: the PQ paper itself showed the split has a big effect. On GIST with $m = 8$, ADC recall@100 was 0.338 with the natural order, 0.286 with a random order and 0.652 with a structured order that groups related histogram bins. OPQ learns such a grouping instead of relying on prior knowledge.

On our synthetic data (already randomly rotated, so slices were balanced) the parametric OPQ rotation lowered MSE from 1.92 to 1.71 at 8 bytes and moved 1-recall@10 from 0.42 to 0.44: a modest gain when variance is already spread out. In Faiss, prefix the factory string with `OPQ16` or `OPQ16_64` (rotate for 16 sub-quantizers and reduce to 64 dims).

**PQ fast scan.** With $k^* = 256$, each scan step reads a table in L1 cache. Andre, Kermarrec and Le Scouarnec (VLDB 2015) observed that cache locality is not enough and moved the tables into SIMD registers. That requires short tables, so codes use 4 bits ($k^* = 16$) and table entries are quantized to 8-bit integers: 16 entries x 8 bits = 128 bits, one vector register. A shuffle instruction then performs many lookups at once.

Faiss implements this as `IndexPQFastScan` and `IndexIVFPQFastScan` (factory `PQ32x4fs`, or `IVF4096,PQ32x4fsr` with residuals). Codes are packed in blocks of 32 vectors and sums are accumulated in 16-bit integers. Faiss recommends pairing 4-bit PQ with re-ranking because it is less accurate than 8-bit PQ at the same memory.

blocks.title: Why 4-bit codes fit a SIMD register lookup

scenes.caption: With k* = 256, one sub-quantizer's table row has 256 float entries (1 KB), read from cache with one lookup per code. Fast scan cannot use this layout.
With k* = 16, the row has 16 entries; quantized to 8-bit integers it is exactly 128 bits. Values shown are illustrative, not from a real query.

A shuffle instruction treats a register of 4-bit codes as indices into the in-register table, looking up many vectors at once. Here code 2 reads position 2 (value 0) and code 7 reads position 7 (value 5).

blocks.md: **Anisotropic quantization (ScaNN).** Guo et al. (ICML 2020) note that for maximum inner product search, the error that matters is the part that changes the score of high-scoring pairs. They split a point's quantization residual $x - \tilde x$ into a component **parallel** to $x$ and one **orthogonal** to it, and show that a score-aware loss weights the parallel part more:

blocks.caption: From Guo et al., for the weight function that counts only inner products above a threshold T. With unit-norm data, T = 0.2 and d = 100, eta = 4.125, the value the paper uses on Glove-1.2M.

blocks.title: How much more ScaNN penalizes parallel error

scenes.caption: At T = 0, every query direction counts equally and the exact eta is 1 (the gray line): ordinary reconstruction loss, which k-means minimizes. The large-d proxy curve reads 0 there, so it is only a guide away from T = 0.
At T = 0.2 with d = 100, parallel error costs 4.125 times as much. Simplified: this uses the large-d limit the paper proposes as a proxy for the exact eta.
Lower d gives a smaller eta at the same T. The codebooks are then learned with this weighted loss instead of plain squared error.

blocks.md: Choosing in practice: if full vectors fit in RAM, HNSW over raw vectors is usually simplest. When memory is the limit, IVF with PQ codes (often with OPQ and fast scan) plus a re-ranking step is the standard recipe, as in Faiss. ScaNN applies the anisotropic loss for inner-product search.

blocks.question: A 4-bit fast-scan index (PQ32x4fs) and an 8-bit index (PQ16) both use 16 bytes per vector. Which statement matches the Faiss docs?
options: Fast scan is faster but less accurate than 8-bit PQ at the same memory, so pair it with re-ranking
They are identical because the bytes are equal
Fast scan is more accurate because it has more sub-quantizers
Fast scan stores float32 tables in registers
blocks.explain: Faiss notes 4-bit PQ is less accurate than 8-bit PQ for the same memory and recommends a refine stage. Its speed comes from 16-entry tables quantized to 8-bit integers, which fit in SIMD registers.

blocks.question: Your embeddings come from a model whose first 32 of 256 dimensions carry most of the variance. Plain PQ with M = 16 has poor recall. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase nprobe
Apply an OPQ rotation before PQ so variance is balanced across sub-spaces

blocks.explain: With the natural split, the first 2 sub-quantizers must represent most of the variance with 256 centroids each, while the rest waste bits. OPQ learns a rotation (for Gaussian data, Eigenvalue Allocation balances eigenvalue products) so each sub-space gets comparable energy. nprobe only matters for IVF list coverage.
